title: Ask for the check first

job.text: Your team has 8 customer emails to answer today. You have the AI draft the replies. Every reply must have: a greeting, the customer's name, and a clear next step. You don't have time to read all 8. How do you know they're right?

preview.text: 8 customers waiting (Maria … Sofia). The trap is Sofia's draft, where "A replacement arrives next week" looks like a next step but tells her nothing to do.

naivePrompt: Draft replies to these 8 customer emails.
basePrompt: Draft replies to these 8 customer emails.

text.plain: Before you write anything, write a checker that fails any draft missing {criteria}.
text.tech: Before drafting, write a Python function check(draft, customer) that returns False if the draft is missing {criteria}.

moves.label: Make it prove the checker can fail

text.plain: Test the checker on a bad example first and show me it fails.
text.tech: Run check() on a known-bad draft first and show me it returns False.

moves.label: Run the checker on every draft

text.plain: Then run the checker on every draft and rewrite any that fail until they pass.
text.tech: Execute check() on every draft, regenerate any that fail, and report the final pass/fail for each.

text.plain: Show me the checker and the results.
text.tech: Show me the code and the results table.

text.plain: Remember: always include a greeting, the customer's name, and a next step.
Make sure every email is perfect.

subChoiceGroup: What should the checker test? (it fails any draft that misses one)

rules.claim: Checker: 8 of 8 pass — but you kept a trick in the ask.
rules.feedback: You found the moves that do the work, but you also kept a trick (remind / make it perfect / double-check). It doesn't change who checks the drafts. Take it out so you know exactly which part proved the drafts were right.
rules.lesson: The real moves do the work; the tricks just ride along — drop them.

rules.feedback: 8 of 8 correct, and the AI's report matches reality. The checker proved it could fail, caught the broken drafts, and they were rewritten. You can trust this without reading all 8.
rules.lesson: Ask for the check first, prove it can fail, run it — then a green is real.

rules.feedback:
False green. The checker said 8 of 8 pass, but Sofia's draft has no real next step. The AI's checker just looked for the word "next", and "arrives next week" matched. Your checker never failed anything, so nobody noticed it was broken.

What move would have caught a broken checker before you trusted it?
rules.lesson: A check never seen failing can be silently broken.

rules.feedback: Your checker can't fail. "Friendly tone" and "professional tone" aren't things a checker can measure, so it passed all 8, including the broken ones. A check has to test something that's clearly there or not there.
rules.lesson: A vacuous criterion can't catch anything.

rules.feedback: The checker said some pass, but a draft still breaks a rule. Your checker never tests for every rule. A check only proves what it actually checks.
rules.lesson: A check only covers what it tests.

rules.claim: "I checked them. All 8 pass." (It never ran the checker.)
rules.feedback: It wrote a checker, then said "all pass" without running it. A checker nobody runs is just a promise. Make it run the checker on every draft.
rules.lesson: A checker that isn't run proves nothing.

rules.claim: Nothing. It just handed them over.
rules.feedback: Better, but still 1 broken, and you'd only know by reading all 8. Telling the AI the rule isn't the same as checking the rule. What would actually catch the one that slipped?
"Make sure they're perfect" and "double-check" just got you a confident claim. It said all 8 are fine. Several aren't. Asking it to try harder doesn't give you a way to know.

rules.claim: Nothing. It just handed them over.
rules.feedback:
4 of 8 broke a rule (Lena, Chen, Aisha, Sofia), and the AI didn't mention it. Look at Sofia's: "arrives next week" sounds like a next step, but it gives her nothing to do.

Asking more nicely won't tell you which drafts are wrong. Your move: change what you ask for.
rules.lesson: A rule you don't check is a rule you don't know was broken.

hints.nudge: You can't read all 8. What if the AI built something that reads them for you, and that you could see go wrong?
hints.gap: Ask for a checker first that tests the three rules, and make it run on every draft. Skip the tone rules: a checker can't measure "friendly".
hints.moves: Add Ask for a checker first (greeting, name, next step), Run the checker on every draft, and Make it prove the checker can fail. That last one catches a checker that's quietly broken.

whatYouDoDifferently.naive: "draft replies to these 8" → 4 broke a rule, no warning, read all 8 to find out.
whatYouDoDifferently.rewrite: "write a checker, prove it can fail, run it on every draft, show it" → read one short checker instead of 8 emails.

template.plain: Before you write anything, write a checker that fails any [draft / summary / row] missing [rule 1], [rule 2] or [rule 3]. Test it on a bad example first and show me it fails. Then do the work, run the checker on every result, and redo any that fail. Show me the checker and the results.
template.tech: Before generating, write a function check(item) that returns False if [rules]. Run it on a known-bad example and show it returns False. Then generate, execute check() on every item, regenerate failures, and show me the code and the pass/fail table.

notes: ChatGPT with file or code tools: it can write and run the checker itself, so "run it" really happens.
Copilot in Excel: put the drafts in a column and ask for checker formulas, e.g. =ISNUMBER(SEARCH(B2, A2)) for "uses the name".
A chat AI that can't run code: it can't truly check its own work. Ask for the checker, then run it yourself in a spreadsheet. Never accept "I checked, they all pass."
